summary: BBN's report on host availability from September 30 to October 8, 1971, with a table of daily test logins. It also notes that three more hosts could now act as servers. It was replaced by RFC 255.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 252 reports host status from September 30 to October 8, 1971, and lists three hosts newly able to act as servers. It also explains the status codes in its daily test table, and RFC 255 later replaced it.

questions: which hosts became servers in the october 1971 report
what did the arpanet host status codes mean
subtitle: An ARPANET host status report covering September 30 to October 8, 1971

tldr.problem: Network users needed updates on which hosts could be reached and which hosts were becoming servers.
tldr.mechanism: The report presents daily host test results and a separate table of status or predictions from site operators.
tldr.outcome: It reports that SRI NIC, MIT Multics and Harvard could now act as servers; RFC 255 later replaced it.

sections.title: The Reporting Period and New Servers
sections.content:
The report covers host status from September 30 through October 8. The BBN prototype Terminal IMP was unavailable from September 27 through September 29 while hardware debugging took place, so the network was not examined on those days.

Three hosts that had not been officially able to act as servers at the time of RFC 240 were now able to do so: SRI NIC's PDP-10, MIT Multics' H-645 and Harvard's PDP-10. The report notes Harvard's limited core space meant it would run Telnet only occasionally.
sections.plainLanguage: The report covers the listed test days and notes why there are no tests for the previous three days. It also says three hosts could now serve other sites.

sections.title: Daily Test Results
sections.content:
The table gives the date, Eastern time and result of tests for each listed host. O means the host opened a connection and was accessible to a user. D means dead or inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP; T means it did not respond, although it was not dead.

R means the host refused the initial request. H means the host opened a connection but immediately closed it or stopped responding. The report marks some sites that said their system might not be available at those times.
sections.plainLanguage: Each table entry describes one attempted connection. The letter codes say whether the host was accessible, unreachable, timed out, refused the request, or only partly opened a connection.

sections.title: Operator Predictions
sections.content:
A separate table lists host status or predictions supplied by site operators. It includes entries such as Server, User only, Soon and dates, along with the person who supplied the information.

The unit metadata records RFC 255 as the document that later obsoleted RFC 252.
sections.plainLanguage: The report also records what operators said about their hosts' roles or expected availability. RFC 255 later replaced it.
